column4: God teaches Adam all the names (الأسماء); this directly joins the section's claim that a name makes its bearer knowable to knowledge granted by God.
Adam tells the angels the names, making the named things a displayed distinction that the angels had not known in 2:31–32.
Its sea, rain, living creatures, winds, and clouds are explicitly signs for people who understand; the created field functions as the section's world of differentiating marks.
The poor are recognized by their سيمى (simah), an outward mark; it is a concrete instance of reading a trace in a person without reducing it to a spoken name.
The angels come مُسَوِّمِينَ, marked in battle. That realizes the source section's dictionary image of a warrior bearing a distinguishing battle mark.
The creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding, directly treating the visible world as something through which one knows.
Stars are set for guidance through land and sea darkness, and the signs are detailed for people who know; elevated visible points make orientation and recognition possible.
The growth and differing ripeness of plants and fruit are presented as signs. Their visible variety supplies the section's claim that created kinds disclose their Maker.
On the elevated A'raf, people recognize every group by their سيمى. Height, a boundary, and readable marks meet in one scene.

God has the most beautiful names and is to be called by them; the command gives the section's account of a divine name as an address with a real referent, while also setting a boundary against those who distort His names.
The sun and phased moon make the count of years and calculation knowable, and are called detailed signs for knowing people; high celestial forms serve legibility rather than mere spectacle.
The alternation of night and day and what God created in the heavens and earth are signs for the God-conscious, extending the section's alamīn image across the created order.
Noah places the Ark's course and mooring under بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ. It is the section's exact image of an action's movement and stopping being placed beneath the Name.
The turning of Lot's town upside down and the rain of stones supplies the destroyed scene whose remaining traces 15:75 asks the مُتَوَسِّمِين to read.
The stones are مُسَوَّمَة, marked by the Lord. The punishment makes the source section's branding/marking sense literal within the same Lot scene.
Adjacent plots, vines, crops, and palms share water yet yield different fruit; the verse makes discernible difference in creation a sign for people who reason.
The upturned town is the concrete ruin immediately interpreted in 15:75 as signs; it grounds the section's image of a catastrophe leaving readable evidence.
The ruined town contains signs for the مُتَوَسِّمِين, those who read marks or traces. This is the Qur'anic realization of the source dictionary sense توسَّم.
Rain-grown crops, olives, dates, grapes, and other fruit are called a sign for people who reflect, making ordinary created variety an intelligible indication.
Night, day, sun, moon, and stars are subjected for human use and are a sign for people who reason; the elevated order becomes readable rather than self-explanatory.
What God has multiplied on earth in differing colors is a sign for those who remember, a close analogue to the section's differentiated created kinds.
God makes علامات and stars by which people are guided. The source section's علم as banner/recognition-mark is enacted by landmarks that make a route knowable.
Allah and "al-Rahman" are both names by which to call, and the most beautiful names belong to Him. It directly joins the two names in the basmalah to invocation.
Worship and patient devotion are followed by the question whether any سميّ can be known for Him. The verse directly binds worship, knowing, and a name-worthy equal as the section says.
The declaration that God has the most beautiful names gives the Name a revealed identity, rather than the empty human labels criticized elsewhere in the section.
The standing sacrificial camels are among God's public symbols, and His name is pronounced over them. An animal becomes a recognizable sacred sign while an act is begun under the Name.
God permits houses to be raised and His name to be remembered in them. The verse explicitly joins elevation with the remembered Name, the section's central double image.
The queen identifies a noble letter that has been delivered to her; this is the receiving scene that 27:30 completes with its sender and the Name under which it speaks.
The letter says it is from Solomon and begins بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ. Its opening functions as the identifying mark of source and authority described in the section.
The deserted houses of the wrongdoers are explicitly an ayah for people who know. Physical ruins are readable traces, paralleling the section's call to see an effect and infer from it.
Noah and the Ark are left as a sign for the worlds. The Ark of 11:41 thus carries both God's Name in its motion and an enduring public mark afterward.
God leaves a clear sign from Lot's city for people who understand. It is the same ruined-place logic as 15:74–75, stated as a visible remainder for readers.
The heavens and earth are created in truth, and that creation is a sign for believers; the verse directly licenses reading the whole created realm as an indication.
Human beings made from dust and then spread abroad are named among God's signs, making a created kind itself a sign rather than an anonymous background.
The creation of spouses and the affection and mercy placed between them are among God's signs, extending the section's created-world image to a human relation.
Differences of languages and colors in the creation of heavens and earth are signs for the knowing (العالمين). Distinction itself here makes recognition and knowledge possible.
Sleep by night and day and seeking bounty are among God's signs; even recurring human experience is presented as a readable form in the created order.
Lightning brings fear and hope, and rain revives the earth; these are named signs for people who understand, where visible effects disclose a hidden giver.
The standing of heaven and earth by God's command is one of His signs. The apparent stability of the world points beyond itself to the command that holds it.
Water produces fruits of varied colors, and mountains have white, red, and intensely black paths. The verse gives concrete visual differentiation within creation.
Human beings, animals, and livestock also differ in color, and the verse turns that attentive perception toward the العلماء. It closely joins differentiated kinds and knowing.
The dead earth brought to life and made to yield grain is expressly an ayah. A changing visible surface becomes a mark from which life-giving power is known.
Night, from which daylight is stripped, is expressly an ayah. The alternating visible boundary makes the order of the world readable.
Carrying their progeny in the laden ship is expressly an ayah. It echoes the Ark scene by presenting the vessel as a public sign, not merely transport.
God will show signs on the horizons and in people themselves until the truth becomes clear. This states the section's central movement from observable mark to recognition.
The creation of the heavens, earth, and creatures dispersed through them is among God's signs; the spread of living kinds is itself an indication.
Ships moving through the sea are likened to الأعلام, great visible landmarks or banners. The image gives the section's flag sense a concrete elevated form.
The heavens and earth contain signs for believers, directly presenting the world as a field of indications.
Human creation and the creatures dispersed through the earth are signs for people of certainty, matching the section's claim that living kinds are themselves signs.
Night and day, descending provision, reviving rain, and turning winds are signs for people who reason; several ordinary phenomena become readable marks together.
The Prophet could recognize hypocrites by their سيمى and by the tenor of their speech. It is a precise Qur'anic instance of discerning good or evil from a trace.
The believers' سيمى is on their faces from the effect of prostration. The verse makes worship leave a recognizable trace, parallel to the section's branded or raised sign.
There are signs on the earth for those with certainty; the earth is explicitly offered as a surface that can be read.
There are signs within yourselves as well. The section's claim that creation functions as a mark therefore includes the human self, not only distant objects.
The clay stones sent against the transgressors are مُسَوَّمَة, marked by the Lord. This repeats 11:83's literal marking in the Lot narrative.
God leaves a sign in the destroyed place for those who fear painful punishment, preserving the ruin as evidence to be read.
The Ark is left as a sign and the verse asks whether anyone will take heed. It turns the vessel named in 11:41 into a durable sign for later readers.
The sea-going ships are like الأعلام, conspicuous high landmarks or banners. This directly recalls the source section's علم as a raised sign.
Blessed is the name of the Lord of majesty and generosity. The verse is the section's direct pairing of the divine Name with exalted greatness.
The command to glorify the name of the tremendous Lord repeats the section's name-and-exaltation stance in a direct imperative.
The same command to glorify the name of the tremendous Lord closes the surah, making the Name the spoken response to what has been shown.
God's creative acts culminate in the statement that His are the most beautiful names. The names identify the Creator whose creatures glorify Him.
The command to glorify the name of the tremendous Lord is another direct instance of the Name being lifted in worship.
Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself wholly to Him. It explicitly couples the Name with the worship and perseverance developed at 19:65.
Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High: name, Lord, and elevation are gathered in the exact sentence developed by the section.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays, making the Name an enacted threshold for worship.
We raised for you your mention gives the source section's secondary sense of a good name lifted among people a direct Qur'anic formulation.
The command to read begins with the name of the creating Lord. It directly realizes the section's claim that reading and beginning take place under the Name.

Not mentioning God's name over slaughter marks a boundary of allegiance and is called disobedience. It clarifies why the section treats beginning under the Name as a real placement, not a decorative formula.

People invent food rules and animals on which they do not mention God's name, fabricating against Him. This is a concrete reversal of the section's true Name making an act intelligible and answerable.
The people of the A'raf recognize particular men by their سيمى and address them about their failed gathering. Their visible mark exposes a condition contrary to the hoped-for good sign.
Hud calls the rivals' deities names that they and their fathers have named without authority. It is the section's false, elevated label with no reality beneath it.
Joseph says that what they worship are only names named by them and their fathers, with no authority sent down. This is the section's explicit contrast between a sign that reveals and an empty label.
When told to prostrate to the Rahman, they reply, "What is the Rahman?" The refusal targets the very divine Name that the basmalah raises as a known sign.

When God alone is mentioned, hearts of those denying the Hereafter recoil, while mention of others pleases them. The opposed reactions show refusal of the Name's referent rather than mere ignorance of a word.
Night, day, sun, and moon are signs, yet the verse forbids prostrating to those signs and directs worship to their Creator. It draws the crucial boundary between a mark and what it makes known.
The verse forbids injurious nicknames and calls the name of wrongdoing after faith wretched. It reverses the source section's good name circulating as a recognizable good trace.
The supposed gods are only names named by people and their fathers, without God-given proof. Like 12:40, it exposes labels whose raised sign has no true referent.
Criminals are recognized by their سيمى and seized by forelocks and feet. The visible mark here is a judicial disclosure of evil, the dark counterpart to reading goodness in a trace.
We shall mark him on the snout makes the source's وسم, a burned or branded identifying trace, literal and punitive.
The angels' admission that they know only what God taught them completes 2:31's naming scene: the names matter because they are taught, differentiating knowledge.
Safa and Marwa are called God's symbols. Physical places serve as publicly recognizable signs within worship, a spatial counterpart to the section's raised marker.
The arrival of the ark is announced as a sign of Saul's kingship. A visible object here certifies an otherwise contested identity and authority.
The House contains clear signs, including Abraham's standing place. A specific place bears a lasting recognizable trace, like the visible marks considered in the section.
Those who remember God reflect on the creation of the heavens and earth in the scene introduced by 3:190. Its own contribution is the act of reading creation rather than treating it as vain.
Hunters are told to mention God's name over what trained animals catch. This gives a practical instance of the source section's act being placed under the Name.
Every land animal and flying bird is a community like humanity. The verse gives the section's claim about created kinds a concrete living plurality.
Believers are told to eat from what God's name has been mentioned over. The Name publicly situates an ordinary act within acknowledged divine authority.
The earth, mountains, rivers, paired fruits, and night/day make the varied natural scene whose differentiating result 13:4 explicitly calls signs.
The destroyed town lies on an established road. Its own contribution is that the trace is publicly passed and can therefore be read by the مُتَوَسِّمِين of 15:75.
The verse calls the immediately preceding ruined-road scene a sign for believers, specifying that the visible trace of 15:74–76 is meant to disclose something.
Rain supplies drinking water and vegetation before 16:11 calls the resulting crop scene a sign; this verse supplies the hidden provision behind the readable growth.
Firm mountains stabilize the earth, then 16:16 names landmarks and guiding stars. Its own contribution is the raised terrain from which a landmark scene emerges.
John is given a name for which no namesake had previously been made. The singular name functions as a distinctive marker rather than an interchangeable sound.
The angels say they descend only by the command of the addressee's Lord; this identifies the speaker and Lord whose unmatched name and worship are stated in 19:65.
Pilgrims mention God's name over provided livestock on appointed days. The ritual gives the section's starting-under-the-Name image a communal, audible form.
Each community has rites so that they mention God's name over the livestock He has provided. The repeated practice joins provision, recognition, and the divine Name.
Pharaoh asks what the Lord of the worlds is. The question opens the section's alamin concern as a question of what the visible worlds point to.
Moses answers that the Lord of the worlds is Lord of the heavens, earth, and what lies between them. It specifies the created field meant by alamin in response to 26:23.
Abraham asks for a truthful mention among later people. It directly develops the source section's secondary sense of a good name travelling among people.
God promises to show His signs and says people will recognize them. This articulates the section's movement from a sign placed before someone to recognition.
People are to be called by their fathers' names, the juster form before God. The command makes naming a disciplined means of recognizing a person's relation rather than an arbitrary tag.
God leaves Noah among later generations. Its own contribution is the preservation of a prophet's honorable mention, the social extension of the raised good name.
The continuing greeting of peace upon Noah gives spoken form to the lasting mention announced in 37:78.
God leaves Abraham among later generations, preserving a good mention that fits the section's account of a name circulating in goodness.
The greeting of peace upon Abraham is the actual lasting utterance that 37:108 says has been left among later people.
God leaves Moses and Aaron among later generations, extending the same enduring good-name scene to both prophets.
The greeting of peace upon Moses and Aaron is the continuing spoken mark of honor prepared by 37:119.
God leaves Elijah among later generations, another explicit instance of honorable remembrance persisting beyond its first bearer.
The greeting of peace upon Elijah gives the lasting mention of 37:129 its visible spoken form.
The messengers are sent with stones of clay; the next ayah identifies those very stones as مُسَوَّمَة. This row supplies the marked object's material scene.
The description begins with "He is Allah," knowing the unseen and seen, and names the Rahman and Rahim. It supplies the identity and names developed into the beautiful names statement in 59:24.
A sequence of divine names fills this ayah, making the names in 59:24 concrete descriptions of the One whom the section says a true name makes known.
Remember the name of your Lord morning and evening. The recurring command makes the Name a sustained orientation of speech and worship.
The freshness of bliss is recognized in faces. Though it does not use the source's technical word وسم, it gives a specific good condition that is read from an outward trace.
The command to look at the camel makes a created living kind an object of attentive recognition, fitting the section's world-as-sign claim.
The command to look at how the sky is raised brings the source's height image into an explicit act of observing creation.
The command to look at mountains set firm presents raised forms as objects through which the reader is meant to perceive.
The command to look at the earth spread out completes the four-part act of reading the created field.
